Maladaptive Strategies.value: go over and over why the event happened to me
I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma

vignette:
Javier owned a successful custom cabinetry business, a world of sawdust, precision, and the satisfying scent of finished wood. At fifty-four, he should have been enjoying the fruits of his labor with his wife, Elena. Instead, he felt like a stranger in his own life, a ghost haunting the edges of his own home. The man who had returned from a six-month stint as a relief worker in a conflict zone two years ago was not the same man who had left. The breaking point had been a moment of unexpected joy: a local charity he'd worked with had sent him a photo of a completed well, and a group of children were laughing as they splashed water. For a fleeting second, Javier felt a warmth spread through his chest, a flicker of the purpose he used to feel. Then, the warmth curdled into ice. The memory surfaced, unbidden and sharp as glass: a similar moment of shared relief at an aid distribution point, the smile of a young girl who had just received a food parcel, a brief, hopeful pause in the chaos. That was the exact moment the first shots had rung out, turning the crowded square into a maelstrom of panic and death. He'd been knocked to the ground, the press of bodies around him both a shield and a suffocating trap.

Now, any hint of positive emotion feels like a harbinger of catastrophe. This profound confusion, where happiness signals imminent danger, has become a potent trigger. It is not the only one. The percussive thud of a nail gun from his workshop can send him to the floor, heart pounding. The simple act of Elena wrapping her arms around him from behind can feel like an assault, a trap closing in. In response to these moments of internal alarm, Javier has developed a rigid set of defenses. After nearly swerving into oncoming traffic when a truck backfired, he began carrying a small, heavy pistol in a holster at the small of his back. The weapon does not make him feel safe; it simply makes the world feel appropriately dangerous, confirming his belief that a threat is always seconds away. When the quiet of an evening at home becomes unbearable, filled with the low hum of his own anxiety, he will pick an argument with Elena. He seizes on some triviality-a bill paid a day late, a misplaced set of keys-and escalates it into a bitter fight. The shouting provides a temporary, if destructive, relief from the silent, looping question that otherwise occupies his mind: Why did it happen to me? Why did I survive when that little girl didn't?

This grim architecture of survival has become its own prison, a self-reinforcing cycle that tightens around him each week. Carrying the weapon has made him perpetually scan his environment for threats, which in turn makes him exquisitely sensitive to the very triggers he is trying to manage. The constant state of high alert means that the physical proximity of a customer leaning over a blueprint, or a friend clapping him on the shoulder, now feels less like a normal interaction and more like a tactical vulnerability. This heightened threat perception only deepens his conviction that he needs the weapon. Similarly, the arguments he instigates to distract himself have eroded the intimacy in his marriage. Elena now moves around him with a cautious hesitancy, her touch tentative. This very distance he has created makes any unexpected attempt at closeness feel even more jarring and threatening, triggering the panicked reaction he dreads and further justifying his emotional withdrawal. The arguments ensure no genuine positive connection can take root, protecting him from the treacherous feeling of happiness while simultaneously starving him of the comfort he desperately needs.

He finally sought help after a disastrous anniversary dinner. Elena had tried to create a perfect evening, a reminder of the life they once had. When she reached across the table and put her hand on his, her eyes full of love, Javier felt the familiar surge of panic. He pulled his hand away as if burned and launched into a cold, cutting critique of the restaurant. The argument that followed in the car on the way home was the worst yet. It ended with Elena's quiet, devastating words: "I don't know who you are anymore, Javi. I feel like I'm living with a loaded gun, and I don't mean the one you carry." The silence that followed was more terrifying than any gunshot. Sitting in the therapist's office for the first time, Javier admits he is afraid of losing his wife, but even more so, he is afraid that the man she once loved is gone for good, replaced by this angry, vigilant stranger.
